title: Blood Relations
summary: One of the highest-yield reasoning topics: family-tree puzzles, pointing-at-photograph statements and symbol-coded chains, all solvable by drawing a small tree with parent-to-child arrows. Marks are lost to direction reversals and assumed genders, never to difficulty. A fixed decoding habit — inside-out for pointing questions, pairwise for coded strings, top-down for statement lists — makes nearly every question here a 30-45 second correct answer.

subtopics.title: How to solve blood-relation questions
subtopics.concept: A blood-relation question gives you a few sentences about one family. Your job is to draw them as a **family tree** and read the answer off it. Two habits protect every mark: never guess a gender, and answer in the direction the question asks. The method below works for every question in this topic.

formulas.name: Mirror pairs
formulas.note: Every relation has a mirror. If A is B's uncle, B is A's nephew or niece.

formulas.name: Marriage words
formulas.note: Spouse's parent = father/mother-in-law. Sibling's spouse or spouse's sibling = brother/sister-in-law.

formulas.name: Cousin
formulas.note: An uncle's or aunt's child is always a cousin, never a nephew.

tricks.title: Write each sentence as an arrow
tricks.body: In the margin, turn every sentence into an arrow: 'Suresh's daughter is Pooja' becomes Suresh to Pooja (F). When every sentence is an arrow, the tree draws itself.

example.q: A is B's sister. C is A's mother. How is C related to B?
steps: Arrows: C to A (F).
A and B sit on one row, so C is above B too.
C is one arrow above B.

tricks.title: Flip the word, not the tree
tricks.body: One tree answers both directions. Keep the drawing, swap to the mirror word: father goes to son, uncle to nephew, grandfather to grandson.

example.q: X is Y's grandmother. How is Y related to X?
steps: Tree: X is two arrows above Y.
Asked from X's side, going down.
Two arrows down, gender of Y decides the word. Y's gender is not fixed.
example.answer: Grandson or granddaughter: cannot be determined

mistakes.wrong: Giving a gender no word stated, like calling every cousin 'he'.
mistakes.right: Mark M or F only from gendered words. Leave the rest blank and let the blank decide the option.

mistakes.wrong: Answering the reverse direction: 'grandfather' when asked how the elder relates to the child.
mistakes.right: Start from the person named after 'related to'. Then walk to the other person.

mistakes.wrong: Calling an uncle's child a nephew.
mistakes.right: Uncle's or aunt's child is a cousin. Nephew is a sibling's child.

mistakes.wrong: Reading 'only son' as 'only child'.
mistakes.right: 'Only son' leaves room for sisters. 'Only child' leaves no sibling at all.

mistakes.wrong: Putting a married couple on different rows.
mistakes.right: A couple always shares one row, one generation.

subtopics.notes:
### What these questions really test
They never test your knowledge of families. They test one skill: turning spoken sentences into a small drawing with zero slips. That drawing is a **family tree**. Build the tree, and the answer is one line.

> **Tip:** Draw every question, even a two-line one. Chains kept in the head cause most wrong answers in this topic.

### The symbols for a tree
Use the same marks every time, so your hand never has to think:

| Mark | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `M` / `F` | male / female |
| `=` | husband and wife |
| arrow down | parent to child |
| one row | brothers and sisters |

Elders sit on the top rows. A child sits one row below its parents. A married couple always shares one row.

> **Rule:** A marriage joins two people of the same row. A child sits one row below its parents.

### Solve in three steps
1. **Mark genders.** Write M or F only where a word fixes it. Father, brother, son, uncle, husband mean male. Mother, sister, daughter, aunt, wife mean female.
2. **Turn each sentence into a link.** "Rita's son is Amit" becomes one arrow, Rita to Amit (M). Take one sentence at a time.
3. **Read the tree.** Find the two people named in the question. Count the arrows between them. Write the relation.

> **Watch:** Cousin, child, parent fix no gender. Leave those names blank. A blank gender is often the whole answer.

### Answer in the asked direction
"How is A related to B?" means: name A **from B's side**. A is B's blank. So start at B, walk to A, and fill the blank.

The same tree answers both directions with mirror words:

| If A is B's... | then B is A's... |
|---|---|
| father / mother | son / daughter |
| grandfather / grandmother | grandson / granddaughter |
| uncle / aunt | nephew / niece |
| cousin | cousin |

> **Watch:** The exam loves to reuse one tree with the question flipped. Read the last line before you mark.

### Count generations on the tree
Every arrow is one generation. Count arrows, then pick the word:

| Arrows between | Going up | Going down |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | father / mother | son / daughter |
| 2 | grandfather / grandmother | grandson / granddaughter |
| 3 | great-grandfather | great-grandson |

Sideways words, the ones students mix up:
- Same parents: brother or sister.
- Parent's brother or sister: uncle or aunt.
- Uncle's or aunt's child: **cousin** (never nephew).
- Sibling's child: nephew (boy) or niece (girl).

### Words that mean "only one"
- **Only child**: no brother and no sister at all.
- **Only son**: no other boy. A sister may still exist.
- **Only daughter**: no other girl. A brother may still exist.

> **Watch:** "Only son" and "only child" build different trees. Read the exact word before you draw.

patterns.name: Which direction is the question asking
patterns.howToSpot: 'How is A related to B?' or the same question flipped: 'How is B related to A?'
steps: Draw the one or two links the statement gives.
Start from the person named after 'related to'. That person is your viewpoint.
Walk the tree to the other person and name them from this side.
patterns.why: The same tree gives opposite words in opposite directions, so fix the viewpoint before naming anything.

example.q: Sunita is the mother of Deepak. How is Deepak related to Sunita?
steps: Arrow: Sunita down to Deepak, marked M.
The question names Sunita after 'related to', so look from her side.
Deepak sits one arrow below Sunita and is male.

patterns.name: Gender never fixed: cannot be determined
patterns.howToSpot: The options include 'Cannot be determined', or the chain ends in a gender-free word like cousin, child, sibling.
steps: Give a gender only to people named by a gendered word (father, sister, wife and so on).
Check whether the asked relation needs a gender that stayed blank.
If it does, choose 'Cannot be determined' or the neutral word.
patterns.why: A relation like son or daughter needs a gender. No statement gave one, so no single option is provable.

example.q: A and B are siblings. C is A's mother. How is B related to C?
steps: B shares a parent with A, so C is B's mother too.
The question now needs B's gender.
No word in the question fixes B's gender.
example.answer: Son or daughter: cannot be determined

patterns.name: Two sentences, one small tree
patterns.howToSpot: Two short sentences, each naming one link, such as 'R is the father of S. T is the sister of S.'
steps: Draw one link per sentence: an arrow for parent and child, one row for siblings.
Merge them: people under the same arrow are siblings.
Read the path between the two named people.
patterns.why: Two links already fix a three-person tree, and the question is just one path on it.

example.q: R is the father of S. T is the sister of S. How is T related to R?
steps: Draw R above S. Put T on S's row, marked F.
Same row means same parents.
T is one arrow below R and female.

patterns.name: Counting members of a family
patterns.howToSpot: 'How many female/male members are there in the family?' after a short description.
steps: Draw every person as a box, including each named husband or wife.
Tick M or F on each box while you draw.
Count the asked group from the drawing, not from memory.
patterns.why: Counting boxes never misses anyone twice; counting from memory usually does.

example.q: A family has a couple, their 3 sons, and 2 daughters of each son. No one else is in the family. How many female members are there?
steps: Females: the wife, that is 1.
Granddaughters: 3 times 2, that is 6.
Total females: 1 + 6.

patterns.name: Mother's side and father's side
patterns.howToSpot: The chain passes through the mother or the father: 'mother's father', 'father's sister', 'maternal uncle'.
steps: Trace one link at a time and draw one arrow per link.
Through the mother = maternal. Through the father = paternal.
Count arrows for the generation, then fix the word with the gender.
patterns.why: A long word only packs three facts: which side, how many arrows, which gender.

example.q: B is the father of A's mother. How is B related to A?
steps: A's mother: one arrow up from A.
Her father: one more arrow up, and male.
Two arrows up through the mother's side.

revision: Draw the tree every time. Never hold a chain in your head.
Gender comes only from gendered words. Blank stays blank.
'How is A related to B?' means name A from B's side.
One arrow = one generation. Two up = grandfather, two down = grandson.
Parent's sibling = uncle or aunt. Their child = cousin. Sibling's child = nephew or niece.
Only son is not only child. Read the exact word.
A blank gender plus 'Cannot be determined' in the options is usually the answer.

subtopics.title: Multi-statement tree puzzles
subtopics.concept: These questions give three to six sentences about one family, in a shuffled order, and then ask a relation. Do not read them in order. Find the oldest person, put them on top, and hang everyone else below. A tree built top-down never needs redoing.

tricks.title: Start from the root
tricks.body: The root is the person nobody calls a child. Build downward from there. Every statement then clicks into an empty slot.

example.q: Rita's son is Amit. Amit's son is Karan. How is Karan related to Rita?
steps: Nobody is called Rita's child except Amit, and Rita is nobody's child. Root: Rita.
Amit one row down, Karan two rows down.
Two arrows down from Rita.

tricks.title: Count arrows, then gender
tricks.body: The arrow count picks the family of the word (father, grandfather, great-grandfather). Only then does gender pick inside it. Never guess the word first and draw later.

example.q: Mohan is Rekha's father. Ramesh is Mohan's father. How is Ramesh related to Rekha?
steps: Rekha, one arrow up: Mohan.
One more arrow up: Ramesh.
Two arrows up, male.

mistakes.wrong: Reading the sentences in exam order and answering from memory.
mistakes.right: Find the root, build top-down, then answer from the tree.

mistakes.wrong: Calling an uncle's or aunt's child a nephew or niece.
mistakes.right: That child is a cousin. A nephew is a sibling's child.

mistakes.wrong: Leaving a spouse out of a count of family members.
mistakes.right: Everyone named, married-in or born-in, gets one box in the tree.

mistakes.wrong: Counting a person whose gender was never fixed.
mistakes.right: Leave blank-gender names out of male and female counts.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing up the two ends of an in-law word.
mistakes.right: Child's spouse is son or daughter-in-law. Spouse's parent is father or mother-in-law.

subtopics.notes:
### What these questions look like
You get three to six sentences about one family. Then comes the ask: how is X related to Y, how many males are there, or who is Z's grandfather.

The sentences are shuffled on purpose. The wife appears before the husband. The grandson appears before the grandfather. Reading them in order and answering from memory is how marks go.

> **Tip:** Treat the sentences as loose parts. Your job is to assemble them into one tree.

### Build the tree from the top
Find the **root**: the person nobody calls a child. Usually a grandfather or a named elder. Put the root on the top row.

1. Hang each named child one row below its parent.
2. Join each husband and wife with `=` on the same row.
3. Repeat until every name in the question sits on the tree.

A tree built this way never needs rework. Each sentence fills an empty slot instead of fighting the earlier ones.

> **Example:** 'Rita's son is Amit. Amit's son is Karan. How is Karan related to Rita?' Root: Rita. One row down: Amit. Two rows down: Karan. Answer: grandson.

### Read relations off the finished tree
Find both people. The relation is the **shortest path** between them, and the direction of each step names it:

| Path from A to B | B is A's... |
|---|---|
| up, up | grandfather / grandmother |
| up | father / mother |
| same row | brother / sister |
| down | son / daughter |
| up, sideways | uncle / aunt (parent's sibling) |
| sideways, down | nephew / niece (sibling's child) |
| up, sideways, down | cousin (parent's sibling's child) |

> **Rule:** Count the up and down steps first. They fix the generation word. Gender only picks between the two words in one cell.

### Every marriage adds a word
Crossing a `=` line changes the ending of the word:

| Crossing | New word |
|---|---|
| child's spouse | son-in-law / daughter-in-law |
| spouse's parent | father-in-law / mother-in-law |
| sibling's spouse, or spouse's sibling | brother-in-law / sister-in-law |

> **Watch:** A spouse joined by marriage still counts in every 'how many members' question.

### Counting males and females
Counting questions are free marks from a finished tree:

1. Write M or F beside each name **while drawing**, only where a word fixes it.
2. Count the asked group by ticking boxes. Include the married-in wives and husbands.
3. Re-read for 'only', 'each' and 'at least'. They change the count.

> **Watch:** Never count a name whose gender stayed blank. That blank is the trap in most counting questions.

### Short chain puzzles
Some puzzles are only two sentences: 'Mohan is Rekha's father. Ramesh is Mohan's father. How is Ramesh related to Rekha?'

Draw the two arrows anyway. Rekha, one arrow up to Mohan, one more up to Ramesh. Two arrows up and male: grandfather. Three arrows would mean great-grandfather. The arrow count picks the family of the word. The gender picks the exact word.

patterns.name: Chains across generations
patterns.howToSpot: Each sentence hangs one person below the last: 'A's son is B, B's daughter is C'.
steps: Draw the chain top-down, one arrow per sentence.
Count arrows between the asked pair: 1 = parent or child, 2 = grand, 3 = great-grand.
Fix the exact word with the gender of the far end.
patterns.why: Generation distance and gender are the only two facts a relation needs, and the chain gives both by counting.

example.q: Ramesh is the father of Vinod. Vinod is the father of Anita. How is Ramesh related to Anita?
steps: Chain: Ramesh, then Vinod, then Anita.
Two arrows from Anita up to Ramesh.
Ramesh is male.

patterns.name: Marriage links: the in-law words
patterns.howToSpot: A wife or husband enters the story, and the asked pair are not blood relatives.
steps: Draw the marriage with = on one row.
Name the plain blood relation of the spouse to the other person.
Swap in the in-law word: child's spouse = son/daughter-in-law, spouse's parent = father/mother-in-law.
patterns.why: Every in-law word is exactly one marriage crossing away from a plain blood word.

example.q: Sneha is the wife of Rita's son Amit. How is Sneha related to Rita?
steps: Amit is Rita's son.
Sneha is married to Rita's child.
Spouse of a child = daughter-in-law, since Sneha is female.

patterns.name: Counting males and females in a family
patterns.howToSpot: A multi-sentence family plus 'How many male/female members are there?'
steps: Draw the full tree, spouses included.
Write M or F beside each name only where a word fixes it.
Count ticks for the asked group. Leave blank-gender names out.
patterns.why: Ticking while drawing turns a memory test into a five-second count.

example.q: Mr. and Mrs. Rao have two sons. The elder son's wife and their two daughters live with them. No one else lives there. How many female members are there?
steps: Females: Mrs. Rao (1), the elder son's wife (1), the two granddaughters (2).
Males: Mr. Rao and the two sons. Not counted.

patterns.name: Shuffled sentences, one tree
patterns.howToSpot: Four to six sentences in a jumbled order, then 'How is X related to Y?'
steps: Find the person nobody calls a child. That is the root.
Attach children below and marriages beside until every name is placed.
Answer from the shortest path between the asked pair.
patterns.why: Shuffled sentences still describe one tree. Building top-down makes each sentence fill one empty slot.

example.q: Anil is the brother of Sunil. Sunil is the father of Mohan. Ritu is the daughter of Kavita. Mohan is the brother of Ritu. How is Kavita related to Anil?
steps: Mohan and Ritu share parents, so Kavita is their mother and Sunil's wife.
Sunil is Anil's brother.
Wife of Anil's brother.

patterns.name: Cousins across two branches
patterns.howToSpot: Grandparents have two married children, and the asked pair come from different branches.
steps: Place the shared grandparent at the top with the two siblings below.
Hang each sibling's children on that sibling's branch.
Children of two siblings are cousins, whatever their genders.
patterns.why: Cousins are exactly the children of siblings. No other path connects two branches.

example.q: Rahul's mother's brother is Vikas. Vikas's daughter is Neha. How is Neha related to Rahul?
steps: Vikas is the brother of Rahul's mother.
Neha is Vikas's child.
Child of a parent's sibling.

revision: Root first: the person nobody calls a child.
Shortest path between the two people = the relation.
Count up and down steps first, gender last.
One marriage crossing adds '-in-law'.
Cousin = child of a parent's sibling, on any side.
Counting: tick genders while drawing. Blanks are never counted.
Spouses count as family members.

subtopics.title: Pointing and introducing
subtopics.concept: 'Pointing to a man, Rita said: he is the only son of my mother's mother's only child.' The whole family hides inside one spoken phrase, and the speaker is part of it. Peel the phrase from the inside out, one link per line. Watch for phrases that fold back on the speaker, like 'my mother's only child'.

tricks.title: One layer per line
tricks.body: Underline the innermost 'my' and work outward. Each line of rough work resolves one 'of'. Then place the speaker and the target in a two-person sketch.

example.q: Pointing to a man, Sunita said: he is the only son of my mother's mother's only child. How is the man related to Sunita?
steps: My mother's mother = maternal grandmother.
Her only child = Sunita's mother.
That mother's only son = Sunita's brother.

tricks.title: Scan for the fold-back
tricks.body: Before peeling anything, scan the phrase for 'my mother's only child', 'my father's only son', 'my mother's only daughter'. If one is there, test the speaker's gender against it first.

example.q: Pointing to Ketan, Meera said: his mother is the only child of my mother. How is Ketan related to Meera?
steps: The only child of Meera's mother is Meera herself.
So Ketan's mother is Meera.
One arrow down.

mistakes.wrong: Reading 'only son' as 'only child'.
mistakes.right: 'Only son' bars other boys only. Sisters may exist.

mistakes.wrong: Forgetting the speaker is a person in the tree.
mistakes.right: Every 'my' belongs to the speaker. Test fold-back phrases first.

mistakes.wrong: Answering in the reverse direction: 'his sister' instead of 'her brother'.
mistakes.right: Check which person the question names after 'related to'.

mistakes.wrong: Peeling a three-layer phrase in one jump.
mistakes.right: One layer per line. Slow rough work is fast here.

mistakes.wrong: Choosing a relation when two families both fit the phrase.
mistakes.right: Build both readings. If both fit, answer 'Cannot be determined'.

subtopics.notes:
### What these questions look like
Someone points at a person and speaks one long phrase. The phrase is the whole question.

> **Example:** 'Pointing to a man, Rita said: he is the only son of my mother's mother's only child. How is the man related to Rita?'

Two people matter: the speaker and the person pointed at. Every 'my' belongs to the speaker. Decode the phrase, place both people, read the relation.

### Peel the phrase from the inside
Work on the innermost 'my' first. Then apply each next 'of' to what you already have. One line of rough work per layer:

1. 'My' = Rita. 'My mother' = Rita's mother.
2. 'My mother's mother' = Rita's maternal grandmother.
3. 'That grandmother's only child' = Rita's mother (she has no sibling).
4. 'The only son of Rita's mother' = Rita's brother.

Answer: the man is Rita's brother.

> **Rule:** Resolve one layer per line. Never collapse two layers into one step. That single slip causes most wrong answers here.

### Phrases that fold back on the speaker
Some phrases end at the speaker:

| Phrase | Means |
|---|---|
| my mother's only child | the speaker |
| my father's only son | the speaker, if the speaker is male |
| my mother's only daughter | the speaker, if the speaker is female |

Test these the moment you see them. The question then becomes a plain one about the speaker's own child, sibling or spouse.

> **Example:** 'He is the son of my father's only son', said by Suresh. Suresh is male, so his father's only son is Suresh himself. The boy is Suresh's son.

> **Watch:** 'My father's only son' spoken by a woman means her brother, not her. Check the speaker's gender first.

### When the answer is 'Cannot be determined'
A phrase fixes only what its words say. If two different families both fit the phrase, no single relation is provable.

Example: 'His wife is the daughter of my grandfather's only child.' The child of the grandfather is the speaker's parent. That parent's daughters are the speaker or her sister. So the man is the speaker's husband, or her sister's husband. Two valid readings, so the answer is **Cannot be determined**.

> **Tip:** Build two small trees instead of arguing. If both fit the words, pick 'Cannot be determined' and move on.

### Blocks the exam reuses
Most phrases are built from a small bank. Learn the bank once:

| Phrase | Decodes to |
|---|---|
| my grandfather's only son | my father |
| my mother's only child | me |
| my father's sister | my aunt |
| my aunt's daughter | my cousin |
| my father's only brother | my uncle |
| my brother's daughter | my niece |

> **Watch:** The word "only" decides who fits. "My father's only son" is me or my brother, depending on my gender.

### Check which direction is asked
Most questions ask how the pointed person relates to the speaker. Some ask the reverse: how is the speaker related to that person. Give the mirror word. If the phrase gives 'he is my brother', the reverse ask is answered with 'I am his sister' (for a female speaker).

patterns.name: Long phrase, decoded layer by layer
patterns.howToSpot: 'Pointing to X, Y said: he or she is the ___ of my ___'s ___', a chain of two or more links.
steps: Replace 'my' with the speaker's name.
Solve the innermost link first, then apply one link at a time, one line per layer.
Name the pointed person's relation to the speaker.
patterns.why: Each layer is one small tree link. Layers solved in order cannot tangle.

example.q: Pointing to a woman, Mohan said: she is the wife of my father's only brother. How is she related to Mohan?
steps: Mohan's father's only brother = Mohan's uncle.
The woman is married to that uncle.
Wife of an uncle.

patterns.name: The phrase returns to the speaker
patterns.howToSpot: The phrase contains 'my mother's only child', 'my father's only son' or 'my mother's only daughter'.
steps: Test the fold-back first: 'my mother's only child' is the speaker.
For 'only son' or 'only daughter', match the speaker's gender. If it fits, the phrase means the speaker.
Reread the sentence with the fold done. It is now about the speaker's own child, sibling or spouse.
patterns.why: The setter hides the simplest family, speaker plus one more person, inside a long phrase.

example.q: Pointing to a boy, Suresh said: he is the son of my father's only son. How is the boy related to Suresh?
steps: Suresh is male. His father's only son = Suresh himself.
The boy is the son of Suresh.
One arrow down from Suresh.

patterns.name: Two readings fit: cannot be determined
patterns.howToSpot: The phrase names a set rather than one person, like 'one of my grandfather's children', and 'Cannot be determined' sits in the options.
steps: Decode the phrase and list every person who could match it.
Check whether the speaker's own gender or an 'only' word removes any of them.
If two different relations stay possible, answer 'Cannot be determined'.
patterns.why: The phrase is genuinely under-specified. Picking one reading is the planted error.

example.q: Pointing to a man, Meena said: his wife is the daughter of my grandfather's only child. How is the man related to Meena?
steps: Grandfather's only child = Meena's mother.
That mother's daughters: Meena, or a sister of Meena.
The man could be Meena's husband or her sister's husband. Both fit.

patterns.name: The reverse ask
patterns.howToSpot: 'How is the speaker related to the person in the photograph?' instead of the usual direction.
steps: Decode the phrase exactly as usual.
Note the direction: speaker to person, not person to speaker.
Give the mirror word of what the phrase produced.
patterns.why: The phrase fixes one relation. The question only asks it from the other end.

example.q: Pointing to a man, Priya said: he is the son of my grandfather's only son. How is Priya related to the man?
steps: Grandfather's only son = Priya's father.
The man is her father's son, so her brother.
Asked from the man's side, going sideways.

revision: Replace 'my' with the speaker's name, then peel one layer per line.
'My mother's only child' = the speaker.
'My father's only son' = the speaker only if the speaker is male.
Only son bars boys. Only daughter bars girls. Only child bars everyone.
Two valid readings = 'Cannot be determined'.
Check the asked direction before writing the word.
Learn the block bank: grandfather's only son, aunt's daughter, father's only brother.

subtopics.title: Coded (symbol) relations
subtopics.concept: The exam invents private symbols: 'P + Q means P is the father of Q'. Then a string like A + B x C hides a small family. Decode one symbol at a time into a plain sentence. Each symbol fixes the gender of its first letter only. Draw the tree, then answer in the question's direction.

tricks.title: Write the sentences under the string
tricks.body: For each symbol, write its one-line sentence under the string, then draw. Six symbols become three short sentences, and the drawing finishes the job.

example.q: 'X % Y' = X is the wife of Y. 'X # Y' = X is the sister of Y. In 'M % N # O', how is M related to O?
steps: M is the wife of N.
N is the sister of O.
M is married to O's sister.

tricks.title: Audit genders before answering
tricks.body: Before marking, list every letter with the gender its symbols fixed. If the asked word needs a gender that stayed blank, the answer is the neutral word or 'Cannot be determined'.

example.q: 'P @ Q' = P is the son of Q. 'P & Q' = P is the husband of Q. In 'P @ Q & R', how is R related to P?
steps: P is Q's son.
Q is R's husband, so Q is male and R is his wife.
R is the wife of P's parent.

mistakes.wrong: Decoding a whole string in one breath.
mistakes.right: Cut at every symbol. One sentence per cut, then draw.

mistakes.wrong: Fixing the gender of the second letter from the symbol.
mistakes.right: 'A is the brother of B' fixes A only. B stays blank until another symbol fixes it.

mistakes.wrong: Answering the string's direction instead of the question's.
mistakes.right: Read the question. If it asks the reverse pair, give the mirror word.

mistakes.wrong: Forgetting the spouse of a parent is also a parent.
mistakes.right: If B is C's wife and B is A's parent, then C is A's parent too.

mistakes.wrong: Marking 'Cannot be determined' without checking every symbol.
mistakes.right: List the gender marks first. Only a truly blank needed gender allows that answer.

subtopics.notes:
### What these questions look like
First come the definitions. Then a coded string, then a question about one pair in it.

> **Example:** 'A + B' means A is the brother of B. 'A x B' means A is the wife of B. In the string **A + B x C**, how is A related to C?

No tree exists yet. You build it from the string, symbol by symbol.

### Decode one symbol at a time
Cut the string at every symbol. Each cut gives one plain sentence:

1. A + B: A is the brother of B.
2. B x C: B is the wife of C.

Now draw. A and B share parents, so A sits beside B. B is married to C, so B and C share a row. Read the asked pair: A is the brother of C's wife, so A is C's **brother-in-law**.

> **Rule:** One symbol = one sentence = one link on the tree. Never decode a whole string in one breath.

### Track each letter's gender
This is the whole game. Every symbol fixes the gender of its **first** letter only:

| Symbol says | First letter becomes |
|---|---|
| father, son, brother, husband, uncle | male |
| mother, daughter, sister, wife, aunt | female |
| sibling, cousin, child, parent | no gender |

In A + B x C with the definitions above: A is male (from +), B is female (from x), C is not fixed by anything.

> **Watch:** If the answer needs a gender nobody fixed, the right reply is the neutral word or 'Cannot be determined'. C, above, could be male or female.

### The same symbol twice adds a generation
A + B + C, with + meaning 'father of', reads as: A is the father of B, and B is the father of C. So A is C's grandfather.

Each repeated parent symbol pushes one more generation. Mixed symbols mix a generation step with a sideways step: parent, then sibling, then spouse, and so on. Draw it. Do not try to feel the answer from the string.

> **Tip:** Under the string, write the gender mark for every letter as you decode it: A + B x C becomes A(m) + B(f) x C(?).

### Answer in the question's direction
Symbols read left to right. Questions read either way.

If A + B means 'A is the father of B', then 'How is A related to B?' is answered **father**, but 'How is B related to A?' needs B's gender. B was fixed only if some other symbol fixed it. Otherwise B is a child of A with no known gender: cannot be determined.

> **Watch:** Most wrong answers here come from answering the string's direction instead of the question's.

### Check your tree before marking
Two quick checks catch almost every slip:
- No person can be their own ancestor.
- Opposite genders for a marriage, where the symbol says husband or wife.

If either check fails, one symbol was decoded backwards. Find it before moving on.

patterns.name: Two symbols, three letters
patterns.howToSpot: Two symbol definitions and a string like A + B x C. One pair's relation is asked.
steps: Translate each symbol into one plain sentence.
Draw the mini tree: siblings share parents, couples share a row.
Read the asked pair, using only the genders the symbols fixed.
patterns.why: Two sentences already form one connected tree, and the answer is a single path on it.

example.q: 'P + Q' means P is the brother of Q. 'P x Q' means P is the wife of Q. In 'A + B x C', how is A related to C?
steps: A is B's brother, so A is male.
B is C's wife, so C is B's husband.
A is the brother of C's wife.

patterns.name: Three symbols, four letters
patterns.howToSpot: Three definitions and a string like A + B - C x D.
steps: Decode left to right, one sentence per symbol, drawing as you go.
Each symbol adds one person. Spouses of parents are parents too.
Answer the asked pair. A gender no symbol fixed means a neutral word.
patterns.why: The string is just three small links. Three small links beat one long guess.

example.q: 'P + Q' = P is the son of Q. 'P - Q' = P is the wife of Q. 'P x Q' = P is the brother of Q. In 'A + B - C x D', how is A related to D?
steps: A is B's son, so A is male.
B is C's wife, so C is A's father.
C is D's brother, so D is A's aunt or uncle. A is D's sibling's son.

patterns.name: Reverse ask on a coded string
patterns.howToSpot: The string runs A ... B ... C but the question asks how C relates to A.
steps: Decode and draw exactly as usual. Do not reverse the string.
Take the viewpoint of the letter named after 'related to'.
Give the mirror word, and check which genders were fixed.
patterns.why: The tree has no direction. Only the final sentence must match the question's direction.

example.q: 'X # Y' means X is the father of Y. 'X @ Y' means X is the sister of Y. In 'A # B @ C', how is C related to A?
steps: A is B's father, and B is C's sister, so A is C's parent too.
Asked from A's side, going down one arrow.
C's gender: no symbol fixed it.
example.answer: Son or daughter: cannot be determined

patterns.name: Build the string for a given relation
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which expression means M is the maternal uncle of K?' The options are strings, not words.
steps: Write the target as plain sentences, middle person included: M is the brother of K's mother.
Pick symbols that state exactly those sentences.
Check each option symbol by symbol. Reject any that changes a gender or a generation.
patterns.why: Each option claims one tree. The correct option must rebuild the target sentences exactly.

example.q: 'P + Q' = P is the brother of Q. 'P - Q' = P is the mother of Q. Which expression means M is the maternal uncle of K?
steps: Needed sentences: M is the brother of some L, and L is the mother of K.
M + L gives the brother sentence. L - K gives the mother sentence.
Joined: M + L - K.

revision: One symbol = one sentence = one tree link.
A symbol fixes the gender of its first letter only.
Parent of one sibling is parent of all the siblings.
Spouse of a parent is also a parent.
Same parent symbol twice = one more generation.
Answer the question's direction, not the string's.
A needed gender that stayed blank = 'Cannot be determined'.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 3-6 shuffled sentences describe one family; the question asks 'How is X related to Y?' or 'How many males are there?'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Ignore the given order. Find the person nobody calls a child, place them at the top, hang children below, join marriages on the same row, and read the shortest path. Tick genders while drawing for counting questions.

example.q: **Anil is the brother of Sunil. Sunil is the father of Mohan. Ritu is the daughter of Kavita. Mohan is the brother of Ritu.** How is Kavita related to Anil?
example.solution: Mohan and Ritu share parents; Ritu's mother is Kavita → Kavita is Sunil's wife → Anil's **sister-in-law**.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Pointing to X, Y said, "He/She is the ___ of my ___'s ___"' — the tree hides in one spoken phrase.
pyqPatterns.approach: Replace 'my' with the speaker's name and decode inside-out, one layer per line. Test the self-reference first ('my mother's only child' = the speaker), then read the final relation in the direction the question asks.

example.q: Pointing to a man, Sunita said, **"He is the only son of my mother's mother's only child."** How is the man related to Sunita?
example.solution: Mother's mother's only child = Sunita's mother; her only son = Sunita's brother → **Brother**.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'P + Q means P is the father of Q...' plus a coded string like A + B × C.
pyqPatterns.approach: Decode one symbol at a time into plain sentences, draw the mini-tree, and mark the gender each symbol fixes (a symbol fixes only its first person). Answer in the question's direction; a blank gender forces a neutral word or 'cannot be determined'.

example.q: '**P + Q**' means P is the son of Q; '**P ÷ Q**' means P is the wife of Q. In '**A + B ÷ C**', how is A related to C?
example.solution: A is B's son and B is C's wife → A is C's **son** (the couple's child).

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Two or three short links in a row: 'A's son is B, B's daughter is C...'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Draw one arrow per sentence, count arrows between the asked pair (1 = parent/child, 2 = grand-, 3 = great-grand-), then fix the exact word with the gender.

example.q: **Mohan is Rekha's father. Ramesh is Mohan's father.** How is Ramesh related to Rekha?
example.solution: Two arrows up from Rekha, male → **Grandfather**.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A full family description plus 'How many male/female members are there?'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Draw the whole tree, write +/− beside every name only where a word fixes the gender (including married-in spouses), then count ticks. Never count a name whose gender stayed blank.

example.q: **Dinesh and Gauri have a son Ashok. Ashok married Nutan; children Pankaj and Seema. Pankaj married Usha; son Tinku. How many males?**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Wives, husbands, in-laws: 'wife of my son', 'father of my spouse', 'brother of my wife'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Apply the in-law map one crossing at a time: spouse's parent = father/mother-in-law; sibling's spouse or spouse's sibling = brother/sister-in-law; child's spouse = son/daughter-in-law.

example.q: **Rita's son is Amit. Amit's wife is Sneha.** How is Sneha related to Rita?
example.solution: Sneha married Rita's child → one crossing from 'daughter' → **daughter-in-law**.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Short statements with 'How is A related to B?' where reversing the direction or guessing a gender gives a plausible wrong option.
pyqPatterns.approach: Start from the person named after 'related to'. Mark genders only where words state them; if the needed gender is blank, pick the neutral option or 'cannot be determined'. Never leave a chain in your head — one arrow per sentence on paper.

example.q: **A and B are siblings. C is the mother of A and B.** How is B related to C?
example.solution: B is C's child, gender never stated → **cannot be determined**.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which expression means M is the maternal uncle of K?' — the options are strings, not words.
pyqPatterns.approach: Write the target relation as two plain sentences ('M is the brother of K's mother'), then match symbols sentence by sentence. Reject options that change a gender or shift a generation.

example.q: '**P + Q**' = P is the brother of Q; '**P − Q**' = P is the mother of Q. Which means 'M is the maternal uncle of K'?
example.solution: Need M = brother of K's mother → **M + L − K** (M is L's brother, L is K's mother).

solvedExamples.q: **A is B's sister. C is the mother of A and B. D is the father of C.** How is A related to D?
solvedExamples.solution: Tree: D → C → (A, B). A is two generations below D and female, so A is D's **granddaughter**. (Daughter skips a generation; niece would need A to be a sibling's child — D has no sibling here.)
solvedExamples.shortcut: Two arrows up from A to D → grandchild; A is female → granddaughter.

solvedExamples.q: **Mohan is Rekha's father. Ramesh is Mohan's father.** How is Ramesh related to Rekha?
solvedExamples.solution: Rekha ↑ Mohan ↑ Ramesh. From Rekha it is two generations up, and Ramesh is male → **grandfather**. Had the question asked 'Rekha is Ramesh's ___', the answer would be granddaughter — direction decides.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Count generations between the pair, then apply the asked direction.

solvedExamples.q: '**P + Q**' means **P is the son of Q** and '**P ÷ Q**' means **P is the wife of Q**. In the expression '**A + B ÷ C**', how is **A related to C**?
solvedExamples.solution: Decode pairwise: A + B → A is the son of B. B ÷ C → B is the wife of C. So A is the son of C's wife, and since B is female and married to C, A is C's **son**. (Grandson would need A to be a generation lower — he is directly B's child.)
solvedExamples.shortcut: Decode pairwise; B's gender from 'wife' is what makes A a son of C, not a step-nephew.

solvedExamples.q: **P and Q are a married couple, P being the husband. R and S are their sons. T is R's wife.** How is **S related to T**?
solvedExamples.solution: S is the brother of R, and T is R's wife — so S is the **brother-in-law** of T (husband's brother).
solvedExamples.shortcut: Spouse's sibling, or sibling's spouse — either route gives brother/sister-in-law.

practice.q: **Suresh and Veena are siblings. Pooja is Suresh's daughter. Rohit is Veena's son.** How is **Rohit related to Pooja**?
practice.solution: Pooja and Rohit are children of siblings — they are **cousins**. (Nephew would need Rohit to be a child of Pooja's brother; uncle would need him to be a brother of Pooja's parent.)
practice.shortcut: Children of siblings = cousins, whatever the genders.

practice.q: **Dhanraj's son is Suresh. Suresh's daughter is Pooja.** How is **Dhanraj related to Pooja**?
practice.solution: Pooja ↑ Suresh ↑ Dhanraj: two generations up, male → **grandfather**.
practice.shortcut: Two up-arrows from Pooja land on Dhanraj — grandparent level.

practice.q: **Rita's son is Amit. Amit's wife is Sneha.** How is **Sneha related to Rita**?
practice.solution: Sneha is the wife of Rita's son → **daughter-in-law**. (Sister-in-law would need Sneha to be a sibling of Rita or of Rita's spouse.)
practice.shortcut: Wife of my child = daughter-in-law; parent of my spouse = mother/father-in-law.

practice.q: **Veena is the sister of Suresh. Pooja is the daughter of Suresh.** How is **Veena related to Pooja**?
practice.solution: Veena is the sister of Pooja's father → Pooja's **aunt**. (Cousin would require Veena to be a *child* of a sibling of Pooja's parent.)
practice.shortcut: Parent's sibling = aunt/uncle; sibling's child = nephew/niece. Keep the two apart.

practice.q: **Kamla is the mother of Veena. Veena's son is Rohit.** How is **Kamla related to Rohit**?
practice.solution: Rohit ↑ Veena ↑ Kamla: two generations up, female → **grandmother** (mother's mother).
practice.shortcut: Maternal or paternal doesn't change the answer — grandparent either way.

practice.q: **Dhanraj and his wife Kamla have two children — Suresh and Veena. Suresh's wife is Rita; their children are Amit and Pooja. Veena's husband is Mohan; their son is Rohit. Amit's wife is Sneha; their son is Karan.** How many **male members** are there in the family?
practice.solution: Males: Dhanraj, Suresh, Mohan, Amit, Rohit, Karan = **6**. Females: Kamla, Rita, Pooja, Sneha, Veena = 5. Tick each gender off the drawn tree, never from memory.
practice.shortcut: Mark +/− beside every name while reading; counting then takes five seconds.

practice.q: Pointing to a man, Sunita said, **"He is the only son of my mother's mother's only child."** How is the man related to Sunita?
practice.solution: Inside-out: my mother's mother's only child = Sunita's mother. Her only son = Sunita's brother. The man is Sunita's **brother**. ('Only son' bars other boys, not other children — Sunita herself is the daughter.)
practice.shortcut: Resolve the innermost 'my ...' first; 'only child' of the maternal grandmother = the mother.

practice.q: Pointing to a woman, Arjun said, **"She is the daughter of my father's father's only son."** How is the woman related to Arjun?
practice.solution: My father's father's only son = Arjun's father. His daughter = Arjun's **sister**. ('Only son' pins the father as the grandfather's sole boy; Arjun's gender is given by his name being male in the sentence.)
practice.shortcut: Grandfather → only son → your own father; his daughter is your sister.

practice.q: Pointing to a man in a photograph, Priya said, **"He is the father of my brother's niece."** How is the man related to Priya?
practice.solution: Priya's brother's niece = a daughter of Priya or of another sibling. Priya is the brother's only sister, so the niece is Priya's own daughter — and her father is Priya's **husband**.
practice.shortcut: 'My brother's niece' = your own daughter (when you are the only sister). Her father = your husband.

practice.q: Pointing to Deepa, Ramesh said, **"She is the daughter of my father's sister."** How is Deepa related to Ramesh?
practice.solution: My father's sister = Ramesh's aunt; her daughter = Ramesh's **cousin**. (Niece is the reverse — the child of one's own sibling.)
practice.shortcut: Aunt's children are cousins; sibling's children are nephews/nieces.

practice.q: '**P + Q**' means **P is the father of Q**; '**P × Q**' means **P is the sister of Q**. In '**A + B × C**', how is **A related to C**?
practice.solution: Decode pairwise: A + B → A is the father of B. B × C → B is the sister of C. Siblings share parents, so A is the father of C too → **Father**. (Grandfather needs an extra generation; none exists here.)
practice.shortcut: Parent of one sibling = parent of all siblings in these puzzles.

practice.q: '**X % Y**' means **X is the wife of Y**; '**X # Y**' means **X is the sister of Y**. In '**M % N # O**', how is **M related to O**?
practice.solution: Decode: M % N → M is the wife of N. N # O → N is the sister of O. So M is the wife of O's sister → M is O's **sister-in-law**.
practice.shortcut: Wife of my sibling = sister-in-law — no gender needed for O.

practice.q: '**P @ Q**' means **P is the son of Q**; '**P & Q**' means **P is the husband of Q**. In '**P @ Q & R**', how is **R related to P**?
practice.solution: Decode: P @ Q → P is the son of Q. Q & R → Q is the husband of R, so Q is male and R is his wife. Q is P's parent, so R — Q's wife — is P's **mother**.
practice.shortcut: The 'husband' symbol pins Q male, which upgrades 'spouse of my parent' to mother.

practice.q: **Rita's son is Amit. Amit's son is Karan.** How is **Karan related to Rita**?
practice.solution: Rita → Amit → Karan: two generations down from Rita, male → **grandson**.
practice.shortcut: Two down-arrows from Rita = grandchild; Karan is a boy → grandson.

practice.q: Introducing a boy, a girl said, **"He is the son of my father's only son."** How is the boy related to the girl?
practice.solution: My father's only son = the girl's brother (the girl is a daughter, so 'only son' is her brother). The boy is her brother's son → her **nephew**.
practice.shortcut: 'Only son' of her father cannot be the girl — she is female — so it is her brother.

practice.q: **Sunita is the mother of Deepak.** How is **Deepak related to Sunita**?
practice.solution: One arrow runs from Sunita down to Deepak. Asked from Sunita's side, Deepak sits one generation below and is male → her **son**. (Brother would need a shared parent with Sunita; nephew needs Deepak to be a sibling's child.)
practice.shortcut: Start from the person named after 'related to'; count arrows from there.

practice.q: **Ravi is the son of Meena. Meena is the daughter of Shobha.** How is **Shobha related to Ravi**?
practice.solution: Ravi ↑ Meena ↑ Shobha: two arrows up from Ravi, and Shobha is female → **grandmother**. (Aunt would need Shobha to be a sibling of a parent.)
practice.shortcut: Two up-arrows = grandparent level; the gender picks the exact word.

practice.q: **P is the husband of Q. R is the father of P.** How is **R related to Q**?
practice.solution: P and Q are married; R is P's father. One marriage crossing from 'father' → R is Q's **father-in-law**.
practice.shortcut: Husband's father = father-in-law; every marriage line adds '-in-law'.

practice.q: **A is the sister of B. C is the mother of A and B.** How is **B related to C**?
practice.solution: B shares C with A, so B is C's child. But no word in the question fixes B's gender ('sibling' words fix nothing) → **cannot be determined**. (Assuming 'brother' because A is a sister is exactly the planted error.)
practice.shortcut: Blank gender = blank answer; 'sister of B' tells us about A, never about B.

practice.q: **M is the son of N. N is the sister of O. O is the father of P.** How is **N related to P**?
practice.solution: O is P's father; N is O's sister. A parent's sister is an **aunt** — N's gender is fixed female by 'sister'. (Uncle is the mirror word; grandmother skips a generation.)
practice.shortcut: Parent's sibling = uncle/aunt; 'sister' pins N female.

practice.q: **X is the mother of Y. Z is the brother of Y. W is the father of X.** How is **W related to Y**?
practice.solution: W → X → Y: two arrows up from Y, and W is male → **grandfather**. Y's own gender is unknown, but the grandparent word never needs it. (Uncle would need W to be a sibling of a parent, not a parent of one.)
practice.shortcut: Count the arrows first; Y's unknown gender does not block this answer.

practice.q: **R is the father of S. T is the sister of S.** How is **T related to R**?
practice.solution: T and S share the parent R, so R → T as well. T is one arrow down from R and female → his **daughter**. (Niece needs T to be a sibling's child.)
practice.shortcut: Siblings hang under the same arrow; one arrow down + female = daughter.

practice.q: **Deepa is the daughter of Manoj. Manoj is the son of Kishan.** How is **Deepa related to Kishan**?
practice.solution: Deepa ↑ Manoj ↑ Kishan: two arrows up from Deepa, and Deepa is female → Kishan's **granddaughter**.
practice.shortcut: Two down-arrows from Kishan land on Deepa — grandchild level.

practice.q: **A is the only daughter of B. B is the mother of C.** How is **C related to A**?
practice.solution: B has exactly one daughter (A), so C must be a **son**. A and C share the mother B → C is A's **brother**. The word 'only daughter' quietly fixes C's gender — that is the whole question.
practice.shortcut: 'Only daughter' = every other child is a boy.

practice.q: **A couple has 3 sons, and each son has 2 daughters. How many female members are in the family?**
practice.solution: Count from the tree: the wife (1) + each son's 2 daughters (3 × 2 = 6) = **7** female members. The husband and the 3 sons are male; nobody else exists.
practice.shortcut: Draw 8 boxes, tick the 7 females — never count in the air.

practice.q: **P and Q are a married couple, P is the husband. R is their son. S is R's wife. T is S's brother. U is R's daughter.** How many **female members** are in the family?
practice.solution: Females: Q (the wife), S (R's wife) and U (R's daughter) = **3**. P, R and T are male — T's gender is fixed by 'brother', so nothing is left blank.
practice.shortcut: Tick a gender under every name first; then the count is one line.

practice.q: **A family has a grandfather and his wife, their son and his wife, and the son's two children — one boy and one girl. How many male members are there?**
practice.solution: Males: the grandfather, the son and the grandson = **3**. The grandmother, the daughter-in-law and the granddaughter are female. Six members in all, split 3 + 3.
practice.shortcut: Two generations of couples plus two children; tick males only.

practice.q: **Anil is the brother of Sunil. Sunil is the father of Mohan. Ritu is the daughter of Kavita. Mohan is the brother of Ritu.** How is **Kavita related to Anil**?
practice.solution: Mohan and Ritu share parents; Ritu's mother is Kavita, so Kavita is Sunil's wife. Wife of Anil's brother → Anil's **sister-in-law**. (Aunt would need Kavita on the parents' generation of Anil — she is on Anil's own row.)
practice.shortcut: Rebuild top-down: the shared-parent sentence joins the scattered names.

practice.q: **Ramesh is the father of Vinod. Vinod is the father of Anita. Anita is the mother of Raju.** How is **Ramesh related to Raju**?
practice.solution: Ramesh → Vinod → Anita → Raju: three arrows up from Raju → great-grandparent level; male → **great-grandfather**. (Grandfather stops one generation short.)
practice.shortcut: Three arrows = great-; two = grand-. Count before naming.

practice.q: **K is the wife of L. M is the father of L.** How is **M related to K**?
practice.solution: M is the father of K's husband → one marriage crossing from 'father' → **father-in-law**.
practice.shortcut: Spouse's parent = mother/father-in-law, every time.

practice.q: **Amit's father is the only son of Ramesh.** How is **Ramesh related to Amit**?
practice.solution: 'The only son of Ramesh' is a child of Ramesh — he is Amit's father. So Ramesh → (Amit's father) → Amit: two arrows up, male → **grandfather**.
practice.shortcut: 'Only son of X' is simply X's child (male); decode it and the chain is short.

practice.q: **Dinesh and his wife Gauri have a son Ashok. Ashok married Nutan; their children are Pankaj and Seema. Pankaj married Usha; their son is Tinku.** How many **male members** are there?
practice.solution: Tick genders on the tree: males are Dinesh, Ashok, Pankaj and Tinku = **4**. Females: Gauri, Nutan, Seema, Usha (4). Eight members in all.
practice.shortcut: One +/− tick per name while reading; the count then takes five seconds.

practice.q: **Rahul's mother's brother is Vikas. Vikas's daughter is Neha.** How is **Neha related to Rahul**?
practice.solution: Vikas is a sibling of Rahul's mother; Neha is his child. Children of siblings → **cousin**. (Niece is the reverse — a sibling's child of Rahul would be Rahul's niece.)
practice.shortcut: Two branches off one grandparent pair = cousins.

practice.q: **A is B's sister. C is B's mother. D is C's father.** How is **A related to D**?
practice.solution: A and B share the mother C; C is D's daughter. So D → C → A: two arrows up from A, and A is female → D's **granddaughter**. (Niece would need A to be a child of D's *sibling* — she is a child of D's child.)
practice.shortcut: Merge the sibling pair first; then it is one straight chain of two arrows.

practice.q: **L is the father of M and N. M is the husband of O. N is the mother of P.** How is **O related to P**?
practice.solution: N is P's mother; M is N's brother; O is M's wife. So O is the wife of P's uncle → P's **aunt** (an aunt by marriage is still the aunt in these puzzles).
practice.shortcut: Hang M and N under L first; the marriage and P slot in around them.

practice.q: **Vijay's wife Reena has a brother Sanjay. Sanjay's wife is Meena.** How is **Reena related to Meena**?
practice.solution: Sanjay is Reena's brother, and Meena married him. A husband's sister is a **sister-in-law** — so Reena is Meena's sister-in-law.
practice.shortcut: Sibling's spouse or spouse's sibling — both crossings give '-in-law'.

practice.q: **Mr. and Mrs. Rao have two sons. The elder son's wife and their two daughters also live with them.** How many **female members** are in the family?
practice.solution: Females: Mrs. Rao, the daughter-in-law, and the two granddaughters = **4**. (Mr. Rao and the two sons are male.) Seven members in total.
practice.shortcut: The two unmarried male sons are the decoys — tick genders, then count.

practice.q: **Sita is the daughter of Ravi. Ravi's sister is Geeta. Geeta's son is Mohan.** How is **Mohan related to Sita**?
practice.solution: Ravi and Geeta are siblings; Sita is Ravi's child and Mohan is Geeta's child. Children of siblings → **cousin**.
practice.shortcut: Spot the married-in branches: each sibling's children are cousins to the other's.

practice.q: Pointing to a girl in a photograph, Rita said, **"She is the daughter of my grandfather's only son."** How is the girl related to Rita?
practice.solution: My grandfather's only son = Rita's father. His daughter = Rita's **sister**. ('Only son' pins the boy as Rita's father, so the girl cannot be a cousin.)
practice.shortcut: Grandfather's only son = your own father — collapse that layer first.

practice.q: Pointing to a woman, Mohan said, **"She is the wife of my father's only brother."** How is the woman related to Mohan?
practice.solution: Father's only brother = Mohan's uncle; the uncle's wife = Mohan's **aunt**.
practice.shortcut: Father's brother = uncle; uncle's wife = aunt. Two blocks, one line.

practice.q: Pointing to a boy, Neha said, **"His mother is the only daughter of my mother."** How is Neha related to the boy?
practice.solution: My mother's only daughter = Neha herself (her mother has exactly one daughter). So the boy's mother **is** Neha → Neha is his **mother**.
practice.shortcut: 'Only daughter of my mother' is the speaker, whenever the speaker is female.

practice.q: Pointing to a boy, Suresh said, **"He is the son of my father's only son."** How is the boy related to Suresh?
practice.solution: Suresh is male, so his father's only son = Suresh himself. The boy is Suresh's **son**. (Nephew would need a second son of the father — 'only son' rules him out.)
practice.shortcut: Self-reference first: father's only son (male speaker) = the speaker.

practice.q: Pointing to a man, Meena said, **"His wife is the daughter of my grandfather's only child."** How is the man related to Meena?
practice.solution: Grandfather's only child = Meena's mother. Her daughters include Meena herself and possibly a sister — the phrase never says the daughter is Meena alone. So the man is Meena's husband **or** her brother-in-law → **cannot be determined**.
practice.shortcut: List every woman who could be 'the daughter'; two candidates → no single relation.

practice.q: Pointing to a man, Deepak said, **"He is the only son of my father."** How is the man related to Deepak?
practice.solution: Deepak is male, and his father has exactly one son — Deepak. So the man in the photo is **Deepak himself**. The question is a mirror, not a family puzzle.
practice.shortcut: 'Only son of my father' + male speaker = the speaker.

practice.q: Pointing to a man, Sita said, **"His mother is the only child of my grandmother."** How is the man related to Sita?
practice.solution: Grandmother's only child = Sita's mother. The man's mother is that same woman → they share a mother → the man is Sita's **brother** (Sita herself is a daughter, so the man is not her).
practice.shortcut: Only child of the grandmother = the mother; her other child is your sibling.

practice.q: Pointing to a man, Pooja said, **"He is the son of one of my grandfather's sons."** How is the man related to Pooja?
practice.solution: Grandfather's sons include Pooja's father and her uncles. The man could be her **brother** (son of her father) or her **cousin** (son of an uncle) — both readings fit the words → **cannot be determined**.
practice.shortcut: 'One of my grandfather's sons' is deliberately unpinned; do not collapse it to 'father'.

practice.q: Pointing to a photograph of a man, Priya said, **"He is the son of my grandfather's only son."** How is **Priya related to the man**?
practice.solution: Grandfather's only son = Priya's father; the man is his son → Priya's brother. The question asks it backwards: Priya is the man's **sister**.
practice.shortcut: Decode as usual, then flip: 'How is the speaker related to X?' wants the mirror word.

practice.q: Pointing to a lady, Geeta said, **"She is the only daughter of my mother's mother."** How is **Geeta related to the lady**?
practice.solution: My mother's mother = Geeta's grandmother; her only daughter = Geeta's mother (the lady). Asked in reverse: Geeta is her **daughter**.
practice.shortcut: Decode the chain to 'mother', then answer the question's own direction.

practice.q: '**P + Q**' means **P is the brother of Q**; '**P − Q**' means **P is the mother of Q**. In '**A + B − C**', how is **A related to C**?
practice.solution: Decode: A is B's brother; B is C's mother. So A is the brother of C's mother → C's **uncle** (A's gender is fixed male by '+').
practice.shortcut: Mother's brother = maternal uncle; the '+' already made A male.

practice.q: '**P × Q**' means **P is the wife of Q**; '**P ÷ Q**' means **P is the sister of Q**. In '**A × B ÷ C**', how is **A related to C**?
practice.solution: A is B's wife; B is C's sister. Wife of the sibling → A is C's **sister-in-law**.
practice.shortcut: Sibling's spouse = brother/sister-in-law; one crossing only.

practice.q: '**P # Q**' means **P is the daughter of Q**; '**P @ Q**' means **P is the father of Q**. In '**A # B @ C**', how is **C related to A**?
practice.solution: A is B's daughter; C is B's child too → A and C share the parent B. But no symbol fixes C's gender → C is A's **brother or sister** (sibling). Choosing 'brother' or 'sister' alone assumes a gender the string never gave.
practice.shortcut: Check which letters got a gender from a symbol; a blank gender forces the neutral word.

practice.q: '**P + Q**' means **P is the son of Q**; '**P − Q**' means **P is the wife of Q**; '**P × Q**' means **P is the brother of Q**. In '**A + B − C × D**', how is **A related to D**?
practice.solution: A is B's son; B is C's wife → C is A's father. C is D's brother → D is a sibling of A's parent. A is male ('son') → A is D's **nephew**.
practice.shortcut: Decode three sentences, draw four boxes; then the path A–C–D is one line.

practice.q: '**P % Q**' means **P is the mother of Q**; '**P & Q**' means **P is the husband of Q**; '**P / Q**' means **P is the sister of Q**. In '**A % B & C / D**', how is **B related to D**?
practice.solution: A is B's mother (so B is male from '&'); B is C's husband; C is D's sister. B is the husband of D's sister → B is D's **brother-in-law**.
practice.shortcut: Husband of my sibling = brother-in-law; the '&'-gender makes B male, so no 'sister-in-law' trap.

practice.q: '**X # Y**' means **X is the father of Y**; '**X @ Y**' means **X is the sister of Y**. In '**A # B @ C**', how is **C related to A**?
practice.solution: A is B's father; B is C's sister → A is C's father too. Asked from C's side: C is A's child — but no symbol fixes C's gender → **son or daughter**. (Grandson invents a generation that does not exist.)
practice.shortcut: Parent of one sibling is parent of all siblings; the gender gap decides the wording.

practice.q: '**P − Q**' means **P is the daughter of Q**; '**P + Q**' means **P is the brother of Q**. In '**C + B − A**', how is **C related to A**?
practice.solution: C is B's brother; B is A's daughter. Siblings share parents, so A is C's parent too — and C is male ('brother') → C is A's **son**. (Nephew would need C to be a sibling's child; C is a direct child here.)
practice.shortcut: Siblings share parents — carry the parent arrow across the '+' before answering.

practice.q: '**P + Q**' means **P is the brother of Q**; '**P − Q**' means **P is the mother of Q**; '**P ÷ Q**' means **P is the father of Q**. Which expression means '**M is the maternal uncle of K**'?
practice.solution: Maternal uncle = mother's brother. 'M + L − K': M is L's brother, L is K's mother ✓. 'M ÷ L − K' makes M a father; 'M − L ÷ K' makes M the mother of K's father (a grandmother); 'M + L + K' makes M K's brother.
practice.shortcut: Write the target as two sentences ('M is L's brother; L is K's mother') and match symbols to them.

practice.q: '**P + Q**' means **P is the son of Q**; '**P @ Q**' means **P is the father of Q**. Which expression means '**P is the grandson of S**'?
practice.solution: Need: P is a son, of someone who is a child of S. 'P + Q + S': P is Q's son and Q is S's son → P is S's **grandson** ✓. 'P @ Q + S' makes P S's father; 'Q + P + S' makes Q the grandson; 'P + Q @ S' makes Q P's father but P S's son (one generation short).
practice.shortcut: Grandson = two 'son' links in a chain — two '+' symbols in a row.

practice.q: '**P − Q**' means **P is the wife of Q**; '**P + Q**' means **P is the brother of Q**. In '**A − B + C − D**', how is **D related to A**?
practice.solution: A is B's wife; B is C's brother; C is D's wife. So D is the husband of A's husband's sister → A's **brother-in-law** (co-brother).
practice.shortcut: Two marriage crossings from A: husband's sister's husband = brother-in-law.
